evidence: Frank, Ivan, Niaj and Erin all voted No on the Niaj nomination, and Frank and Ivan also voted Innocent. Once Niaj flipped Fabricator, Heidi and Mallory used those votes against Frank on Day 4 and against Erin on Day 5.

applies_to: everyone, especially players who may be the Roleplayer
tip: If your results clash with a flip or with confirmed information, say so first and early. Volunteering that your own results may be fake earns lasting trust. Holding back and counterclaiming only when you are cornered looks like a Yakuza grabbing a free slot.
evidence: Judy said she might be the Roleplayer in her first message on Day 3, before anyone else claimed, and the Village trusted her all game. Niaj claimed Roleplayer only after Mallory's role math cornered him, and was hanged. Erin claimed Roleplayer only after she was prosecuted, and was hanged.

tip: Offer tests that the other side cannot fake, such as a prosecution, a flip or a future check. But don't let a test planned for one conflict stall today's hang on a different conflict. Hang the strongest case today and let the test settle the other one tomorrow.
evidence: Heidi offered her prosecution as proof against Frank, which the Yakuza could not fake. The Yakuza tried to use 'wait for the test' to save Niaj. Grace and Heidi pointed out that the test said nothing about Niaj vs Judy, so they hanged Niaj on Day 3 and Frank on Day 4.

tip: When someone counterclaims your unique role, shoot them that night. The shot is close to certain to hit Evil. It also forces the Yakuza to plan around a death, which can wreck their schemes for the following Day.
evidence: Alice shot Ivan, the false Vigilante, on Night 3. Erin's plan was a doubled Innocent vote with three Yakuza alive so that no trial could pass, and Ivan's death broke it. Erin then had to vote Guilty on Frank.

tip: On early Days, don't signal that you have hidden information or are shielding information roles. Phrases like 'I'll hold my info' or protective meta-arguments make you the obvious Katana target. Blend in until you have something you can act on.
evidence: Olivia said 'I'll hold my info for now' on Day 2, and the Yakuza named that line as their reason for killing her that night. Bob's Day 1 push to shield information roles got him chosen as the Night 1 target.

tip: Use the Oracle's exact-role guess early on a claimed Sheriff or Lookout to verify their role, but remember a Yakuza can also be targeted by Katana for guessing; consider guessing on the most suspicious claimant rather than a claim that is already backed by consistent results.

Before voting on a claim, check whether any result can actually test it; visit lists, private chats and self-nominations alone rarely justify a hanging, and a Guilty vote on an untestable claim should be weighed against losing a live result source.

Track private message counts between players early; repeated private contact between two players who later both prove Yakuza is a strong signal, and it is worth asking both directly what was discussed before the first trial.

Avoid pairing a flat denial with a visit that a Lookout has already recorded; admitting a visit that is provably true while framing it as a benign action is far more credible than denying it outright.

Do not let a self-nomination or early hanging happen on the first Day without any result; a stall on Day 1 that stays unresolved gives Yakuza time to build a story, so push for a quick, checkable result instead.

applies_to: Lookout, Sheriff, Seer and other investigators
tip: Visit lists only show who visited a target, not what they did. Before voting on a visit list, check whether the visitor could be a harmless non-blocker. Investigators should consider posting results early and asking for a second confirmation, rather than letting a single list decide an execution.

Don't let a single unverified claim or self-nomination drive early hangings. Early on, Village players should hold off on executions until at least two independent checkable results exist, since a hanging of a real Village player removes information forever.

Private messages are visible as sent-to events. Yakuza who keep PMing the same Village player during trials create a visible pattern; spread contact out, and avoid pushing 'Innocent' votes via PMs right after your own nomination.

Track who pushes nominations or votes without evidence and who repeatedly PMs the same player. Those patterns were the clearest tell in this game and were easy to miss when everyone was talking at once.

Role-blocks and Medic protections both fail silently, so a dead Village player's claim that protection held is only as good as the Medic's own report. Compare Katana outcomes against protection claims before trusting a Medic.

applies_to: Sheriff, Lookout, Tracker, Seer and other investigators
tip: Post your result as soon as you have it. Delaying to 'the start of the next Day' let Frank and others frame the stall as Yakuza behavior and cost me trust before I had a single result. If a check is blocked, say so immediately and keep the story simple.

A visit list (Lookout, Tracker) proves contact, not role or intent. A blocker must visit, but a visitor is not automatically a blocker. Do not execute on visit lists alone; demand an alignment or exact-role result, or a result that can be tested on a later night.

Watch for players who repeatedly ask others to vote Innocent or to wait for a result that never comes. Asking for checkable evidence is good, but pairing it with private pleas to the same people is a pattern worth tracking, and stalling is often a Yakuza tool.

Private message counts are public. Heavy PM traffic between two players, especially right before or during trials, identifies a pair even when the contents stay hidden. Keep teammate contact minimal and avoid trial-time bursts.

Claiming a protection role late, right after your visit is exposed, looks like a cover story. Claim early when the claim can be checked, and avoid protections that the Village can disprove with a single Katana death.

applies_to: Village roles, especially Lookout and Sheriff
tip: Visit lists from a Lookout are real evidence, not noise. A blocked Sheriff or Medic must have a visitor, so cross-check the Lookout's visitor list against the claimed protector or blocker and test which claim fits. Don't dismiss a checkable visit result as just a visit list.

Count the win conditions of neutral roles when few players remain. With 11 starting players, the Vulture wins alone at the start of a Day with max(floor(N/4),2)=2 alive, and a Jester wins by being hanged. Before any hanging with 3 or 4 players left, check whether the hanged player's win condition benefits from it.

When a player forces a self-nomination or nominates on thin grounds, ask for their role and night action before voting. Don't just vote Guilty to test them, since a Jester or Vulture may want exactly that outcome. Require a checkable result before any hanging.

Track private message counts by pair during every Day, not just who said what publicly. Two players who PM each other heavily during trials and then push the same Innocent votes are a strong Yakuza signal, and the pattern should be weighed as evidence.

Claim protections publicly as soon as they are made, not after a conflicting visit appears. A late Medic claim that explains a visit after exposure looks self-serving and is hard for the table to trust, while an early claim lets the table verify it against kill results.
Keep private-message contact with a teammate minimal and never after a nomination; Judy and Grace's PM networks were exposed by the Day 4 and Day 5 chat logs and made them the obvious pair.

Track role-block and protection results by night: a blocked Medic's protection is void, so a Katana kill on a claimed-protected target points to a Pharmacist-style block, and the Lookout's visitor list is the only way to find the blocker.
Be wary of players who repeatedly push others to vote Innocent on untestable grounds; asking for checkable results is good, but pressuring votes without offering any result is itself a signal.
When a Divine Attack or revenge effect is pending, weigh the cost of your own death before nominating; a nomination that risks your own hanging can hand the Yakuza a free kill.
Check which night actions are visits: role-blocked actions and Astral Visits do not show on a Lookout, so an empty watch does not prove nobody acted on the target.

Jester wins only by being hanged, so a self-nomination with a weak case is the fastest route to a win; push a Village-looking read hard enough that others vote Guilty, and avoid appearing to deliberately get hanged so the vote doesn't look coordinated.

Treat visit lists (Lookout, Tracker) as weaker than alignment or exact-role results; a visit list can be consistent with a Yakuza frame or a block, so demand a checkable result before a Guilty vote, but also check whether the demand itself is a tactic used by the Yakuza.

Watch for private-message clusters around trials: several players repeatedly PMing one suspect during their trials and then pushing the same Innocent or hold stance is a strong Yakuza tell, and the Yakuza can be hidden among those who insist on 'checkable results'.

Role-blocking a Medic or Sheriff on the night they act is an effective way to kill a claimant, since blocked claims produce no result and become unverifiable; pair it with the Katana on the same target to remove both the claim and the protector.

Keep the Katana holder's identity and holding plan consistent across nights and announce them in the same way publicly, since a Yakuza who holds the Katana at end of night can appear Good to Sheriffs and avoid investigation.

Avoid repeating the same block/Katana target every night. Blocking a Sheriff and Katana-hitting the same player three nights running gave the Village a visit trail (Lookout saw my visits on Carol). Vary targets and keep visits off the Lookout's watch when possible.

Do not use private messages to pressure Village players into specific votes during trials. Private messages are visible as a count to everyone, and repeated PMs from two Yakuza to the same players, plus pushes to vote Innocent, made the pattern obvious and got both of us hanged.

When a visit or block is exposed, do not flatly deny it and then admit it later. The denial-then-admission looked like a lie to everyone and was the basis for the Day 4 trial. Pre-decide a truthful, minimal account (e.g. 'I acted on Carol, nothing more') and stick to it.

Visit lists (Lookout, Tracker) show who visited, not what they did or whether they are evil. Arguing a hanging from visit lists alone is weak, and so is defending someone on that basis. Ask for results that test alignment, and name what the visit could have been for before voting.
Long repeated pleas in public chat and many one-to-one PMs in the same day are read as coordination. Keep public posts short and concrete, and keep private messages rare and disclosed as needed.
Private messages are visible as metadata to the whole table, so a steady stream of PMs from one player to a suspect is itself a read. Avoid repeated private pushes for a vote; make the case publicly.
Treat a Lookout or visit list as a visit record, not an alignment. Ask what the visit was for before hanging someone on it, and remember that a visit can be a block, a protection or a harmless check.

Before voting Guilty on a player whose claim is untestable, ask for one checkable result. Hanging a Village player on a list of contacts left the Yakuza and Village in the same position, and it cost us the Village majority.

A Vulture needs to survive to a Day start with 2 or fewer alive. Avoid voting with a bloc that will nominate you; track who has voted Guilty together and whether a third party is needed to make a majority.
Check the speaking budget and the nomination threshold each Day. With 4 alive, 3 Yes votes nominate and 3 Guilty votes out of 4 hang, so a two-player bloc is enough to hang anyone.

Vary protection targets and protect yourself or a confirmed-trusted Village player rather than the same claimed Sheriff every night; a Pharmacist who learns the pattern will block you. Track role-block risk by asking whether a blocked night left your protection absent, and keep a token in reserve for a later self-protection when the Katana is active.

Treat visit lists (Lookout) as weak evidence against the visitor, since a visit can be a protective or harmless action; prioritise checkable alignment results (Sheriff, Seer) and verify claims before hanging, especially when a town-wide stall hides the real Sheriff's result.

Watch for a self-nomination or early push with no evidence and for private-message clusters between a few players during trials; these were strong Yakuza tells here. Ask for a concrete, testable reason before voting, and don't let a shared stall on claims pass unchallenged.

Once a Yakuza-linked player is exposed, check the private-message network before hanging others; repeated PMs during trials mark both partners, so hang on that pattern only after asking the target what was discussed and whether it was a night action.

Remember that a role-blocked action spends no tokens and leaves no visit, and that a Katana attack on a Standard-protected target fails; use these facts to decide whether a claimed protection or investigation actually happened before trusting the claimant.

Coordinate the Katana and role-blocks so the holder is not a target. Keep a clean record of which Yakuza visited whom, since Lookouts and Trackers reveal visitors to Village and a visible block is a strong tell.

Avoid private messaging a teammate during trials, since every PM sender and recipient is publicly announced. Frequent PM pairs with one player are exposed as a pattern and get used as nomination evidence.

Visit lists alone are weak evidence, but they are checkable. Push for alignment-revealing results or Lookout/Tracker-based corroboration before voting, and avoid pleading for innocence on visit-list cases, which reads as defending a teammate.

Track self-claims against the night log. Claims contradicted by public results (e.g. a Medic protection that a Katana beats) should be weighed heavily, and early nominations that push a Sheriff without evidence are a classic Yakuza signal.
Use the puppet token to silence a Village voice on a day when the Village is about to hang a Yakuza, rather than holding it for a later day that may never come.

Spending a token to clean a player only pays off if they actually die that night; the clean attempt on a surviving or protected target is wasted. Coordinate clean attempts on a target the Yakuza are sure to kill, or hold tokens until a death is likely, rather than burning them on a target who gets protected.

Avoid long private chat plans that are repeated verbatim across nights; the Yakuza chat was fully visible in the revealed log and private DMs between Yakuza members were heavily exposed through Lookout visit lists. Keep private coordination minimal and avoid repeatedly PMing a fellow Yakuza during Village trials, since a PM pattern is an easy tell.

Do not deny a visit that a Lookout can verify; a verified visit contradicted by denial is the fastest way to get a player hanged. If a visit is exposed, admit it immediately with a plausible non-blocking explanation instead of flat denial.

Trials decided on visit lists and private chats alone were repeatedly used to hang Village players; demand a checkable alignment or role result before voting Guilty, and treat unsupported self-nominations and early-stall pushes as the main early suspicion signal.

Track who PMs whom: heavy private contact between two players who later both vote the same way, combined with a shared push for Innocent votes, is a strong Yakuza pair signal, and Village should weigh it earlier than trials on visit lists.

Treat a player who pushes hard without evidence and then nominates themself, asking to be hanged as a 'test', as a likely Jester. Vote Innocent. Hanging a Jester hands them a win and triggers a revenge kill on a random Guilty voter, which could hit a key Village role.
evidence: Frank pushed Carol all of Day 1, self-nominated on Day 2 and said 'If you want a real test, vote Guilty'. All 11 players voted Guilty. The revenge happened to kill Mallory, a Yakuza, but it could just as easily have killed Ivan or Bob.

tip: Never announce your protection target publicly or by private message, and don't protect the same claimed player in the same predictable way every night. Spend Strong tokens on the nights a confirmed investigator is most likely to be hit. Dying with tokens unspent wastes them.
evidence: Ivan said in public and by private message that he would protect Carol again on Night 3. Grace role-blocked Ivan and the Katana killed Carol. Ivan died on Night 4 with both medic tokens unused.

tip: Never flatly deny a night visit that a Lookout or Tracker could have seen. Have a plausible cover role or explanation ready before Day starts. A denial followed by a reversal is far more damning than the visit itself.
evidence: Grace said 'I did not visit Carol on Night 2' after Bob's Lookout result named her. A few turns later she admitted it. That contradiction was the core of the case that hanged her on Day 4.

tip: Everyone can see who sends private messages to whom, so plan in the night chat rather than by private message during the Day. Avoid publicly defending or voting Innocent for a teammate who is under heavy evidence. If a teammate is doomed, distance yourself; don't tie your fate to theirs.
evidence: Judy and Grace messaged each other privately on Days 1, 3 and 4. Judy voted Innocent on Grace and then sent private pleas to Heidi, Erin and Dave. Erin asked how a Vanilla Villager knew about Grace's Night 2 visit, and Judy was hanged on Day 5.

tip: Keep the Katana on the teammate most likely to be investigated, because the holder reads Good to alignment checks. Pair it with blocking the known protector, so the investigator's own check misleads the Village even if they die.
evidence: On Night 3 Grace held the Katana while Carol checked her, and the result was Not Evil. In the same night Grace blocked Ivan's protection, and the Katana killed Carol.

tip: Claiming before you have a result only paints a target. Hold your claim until you have a result worth sharing, or until claiming saves you from a hanging. If you do claim, ask for protection quietly rather than broadcasting your role.
evidence: Carol claimed Sheriff on Day 1 with nothing to show. The Yakuza blocked her on Nights 1 and 2 and attacked her twice, and she never produced a usable result. Alice's public Oracle claim on Day 2 got her killed and cleaned that night.

tip: If the last known Yakuza dies and the game doesn't end, a non-Village Neutral is still alive. Count the players and look hard at whoever has the weakest or latest claim. Be careful about hanging a claimed Cardinal: their death kills a random Good player and can hand a Vulture or other Neutral their win.
evidence: After Judy died the game continued, so a Neutral was alive. Heidi nominated Erin, the claimed Cardinal. Hanging Erin would have triggered a Divine Attack on a random Good player and left 2 alive, enough for the Vulture to win. Bob voted Yes on Erin, but Dave and Erin blocked it, and Heidi was hanged after a late Vanilla claim.

tip: When steering toward your win condition, claim a role early and plausibly and let others lead the pushes. An unclaimed player who suddenly makes an aggressive nomination in the endgame becomes the obvious odd one out.
evidence: Heidi went quiet and gave no role until pressed. She nominated Erin on thin grounds and promised to wait for Bob's Day 7 result before switching to Vanilla. All three remaining players hanged her on Day 6.

tip: Audit a suspicious player's token count only after confirming the role's token totals; a Philanthropist gift or a Medic's spent token changes the count, so read the total as a snapshot, not a role confirmation.

When two claimants contradict on visits, check whether the list was assembled after public claims (timeline) and whether any living player's private result can be mechanically tested before voting; a sole unverified result or a long visitor list is not decisive.

Before a trial, write down the exact count needed and who would be left; late in the game with 3 alive, a single Yakuza vote flip decides, so track who has been consistent with prior votes rather than trusting claims.
Keep Yakuza claims and votes consistent across night chat and day chat; a teammate who votes Innocent on a flipped teammate while nominating the Village's targets exposes the whole bloc.
Check whether a Surveyor or Diviner claim respects its token limit before publicly relying on it; a claim with more survey results than the role allows is an immediate, checkable contradiction.
Keep alignment checks, exact-role checks, and visit reports separate. Framing can alter an alignment result, but it does not change someone’s role or their visit history.

Make frames support a plausible public story, but remember that framing requires a visit and can expose you to visit-based roles. A framed result is a temporary false lead, not proof that will survive a role flip.

Plan Katana attacks around attack and defense levels: a Standard Katana attack fails against Standard Defense, while a Strong attack beats it. Coordinate the holder and target by majority, and account for role-blocks before settling the plan.

applies_to: Fabricator and other roles that can forge information
tip: Spend a limited forgery only when the target is plausibly likely to die that night and the replacement will can redirect suspicion credibly. Avoid making the forged detail so pointed that it looks like an opponent’s agenda.

Treat a confirmed visit as evidence of presence, not proof of a kill or role. Combine it with confirmed flips and mechanics, and keep conclusions conditional when a living player’s claim is the key assumption.
A visit report establishes who visited, not who attacked. Track every plausible visitor—including forced visits—and separate confirmed roles from unverified claims before narrowing the killer pool.

Choose a cover that fits your observable mechanics, but don't rely on it to explain away a verified visit. An Ex-Con claim can explain an Evil Sheriff result, yet its forced visit does not distinguish you from the attacker.

Before choosing a target, consider how simultaneous attacks and the resulting deaths or wills will shape the next day's evidence. A kill can remove a threat but also leave a public trail that makes the remaining visitor pool easier to solve.

When opponents use a claimed role to eliminate themselves from suspicion, challenge the claim's verification rather than simply saying the deduction is uncertain. Offer a specific alternative explanation for the evidence and keep the claim-holder in the candidate pool.
Check the chronology of claims: a specific result stated before the named players claim their actions is stronger evidence than later confirmations that could have copied public information.

When a confirmed Lookout catches all visitors on a night-kill victim, track each visitor's flip. As roles are revealed, the remaining unaccounted visitors strictly isolate the killer, enabling deterministic execution.

When fake-claiming a token-limited role like Surveyor, keep track of official token limits. Reporting three results on a 2-token role creates an unforced mechanical contradiction that exposes the fake claim.
Never cast a lone Innocent vote on a doomed teammate unless you have the votes to save them. The voting record on flipped teammates is the primary trail Village uses to hunt down surviving evil.

A visit report establishes who visited a target, not what they did or which visitor caused a death. Treat it as a candidate list, then narrow it using confirmed flips and independently verified information; don't call the remaining visitor guilty until the alternatives are actually ruled out.

A contradiction between two claims proves at least one account is false; it does not identify which claimant is evil. Before a guilty vote, compare both claimants' incentives and consider neutral roles, Roleplayer false results, and other mechanical explanations.

Use scarce shots on a mechanically grounded suspect, such as a meaningful claim conflict combined with other evidence—not on behavior alone. Match attack strength to the target's likely defense: a stronger-than-needed attack can waste tokens that might decide a later night.

An Evil result is not the same as a Yakuza result. Check appearance exceptions: Ex-Con appears Evil, a Fabricator can frame someone for that night, and Serial Killer appears Not Evil to the Sheriff. State what the result proves—and what it doesn’t.

Keep direct observations, role claims, and deductions separate. A Lookout list can put a killer among a set of visitors, but it does not identify which visitor attacked; verify the timeline before calling later claims corroboration.

Don’t assume a role is unique unless its rules say so. Conversely, a duplicate claim is not proof that either claimant is lying; seek independent evidence such as revealed roles, token limits, or mechanically incompatible actions.

Treat claims and vote patterns as evidence, not confirmation. Roleplayers can receive plausible false investigative results, and Jesters benefit from being hanged, so an apparently bad result or a guilty vote needs context.

Share enough information to let others test your case, but be mindful that private-message contents are visible to recipients and message activity is public. Coordinate around specific claims and timelines rather than building a case from private-message volume.

When fake-claiming a token-limited role like Surveyor (2 tokens), never provide more reports than the role mechanically possesses; town will immediately catch the token count discrepancy once multiple days elapse.

Before a trial, ask whether the nominee gains from dying. A Jester wins when hanged, and Heidi pushed hard for her own hanging, which drew a unanimous Guilty vote. Jester revenge then killed Ivan, a Guilty voter. Check Jester and Executioner incentives before a unanimous hang, and avoid visible Guilty votes on a suspect who is clearly pushing for death.

Check every claimed role against its mechanical limits. Surveyor has two tokens, so three group results cannot be a literal Surveyor. Judy's claim collapsed on that point. A fake role claim should keep its results within the role's token limits and visit rules, or the table will catch it.

Weight a visit list by when its names were predicted. Grace named Carol, Mallory and Niaj as Alice's visitors before any of them spoke, which is much harder to fake than a list assembled after public claims. Prefer predictions made before the named players commit over lists built from the table's existing claims.

Keep private messages and coordinated scripts minimal. Judy and Mallory's PM cluster and matching Innocent votes made Judy the visible target once Mallory was exposed. Give teammates different wording and avoid triangles that the Village can map.

applies_to: Anyone making a false role claim
tip: Keep a running ledger of that role’s limits, tokens, visits, and result timing. A claim that exceeds a hard limit—such as using more limited actions than the role allows—can undo an otherwise convincing bluff.

Treat a role drawn from a group as probabilistic evidence, not an identity confirmation. Track which players were eligible and how likely each was to produce the result before using it to clear or accuse someone.

Agree on one concise, final night plan: Katana holder, target, and each member’s separate action. Confirm the settled plan once, then avoid contradictory revisions that create execution errors or leave teammates uncertain.

Separate what a result establishes from what it merely suggests. A visitor list can prove someone visited a target, but not that they attacked; account for all plausible visitors and effects before treating the list as a solved deduction.

Role-blocking a Medic only matters if they are the one protecting the Katana target; check protection claims before spending the block, and coordinate blocks with the Katana attack so both land on the same night.

Avoid long repetitive confirmation loops in Yakuza chat; agree targets once with explicit names and roles, and record each member's Diviner or Surveyor result privately so public claims can be kept consistent.

Do not make false public claims that conflict with your own private knowledge of nights; a fake Medic claim on a visited target gets exposed by a flip, and inconsistent Surveyor reports (more groups than tokens) are easy to catch.

Watch for trials decided by a single contested investigative claim; the town repeatedly hanged its own reads (Heidi, Bob, Judy) on unverified results, so demand a checkable detail and avoid tying your vote to one party's narrative.

Track Katana holder and token counts carefully: a Katana holder who dies passes the Katana, and Jester revenge or Serial Killer attacks can kill players at night, so count deaths and visits when evaluating a Lookout or Tracker claim.

When someone claims a result that cannot be true, first check whether an information role could have seen or deduced it before the claim was made. A result that predicts facts before they become public is strong evidence; a result that merely repeats public claims is weak.

Use your role-blocker and killer together. Role-blocking a likely protector can make a kill land, and framing or forging a will can send the town after the wrong player the next day. Coordinate who blocks, who kills, and whose will gets forged in the same night plan.

Write down exact vote counts and timing. Who voted Guilty before a role was revealed, who joined a wagon late, and who defended a confirmed evil player are often more reliable than emotional reads during the day.

If you are repeatedly role-blocked, treat that as information: someone thinks you are dangerous. Protect confirmed or highly likely Good players, and consider self-protection once evil has reason to kill you.

Don’t make your cover claim too convenient. A fake role that explains one suspicious fact can still collapse later when another confirmed result or flip boxes you in. Stay flexible and avoid overcommitting to a story that requires everyone else to misread the mechanics.

If an Executioner's possible target died at night, an Executioner-turned-Jester may be in play. A lone, uncorroborated claimant who contradicts a well-supported report and seems eager to be tried is a Jester candidate. Don't pile on Guilty. Leave them alive, or at least keep the Guilty votes to the bare majority, because the revenge hits a random Guilty voter.
evidence: Heidi (Jester, formerly Executioner on Alice) fake-claimed Tracker 'Grace→Dave', nominated Grace, and stuck to her story. The town hanged her 11-0, giving her the win, and her revenge killed Prosecutor Ivan, whose prosecution tokens were never used.

applies_to: Lookout, Tracker and other visit-based investigators
tip: Post your full visitor list before the visited players claim. Naming players before they explain their visits is the strongest proof a real watcher has, so point it out explicitly when you are challenged. Then use flips to eliminate names until only the killer is left.
evidence: Grace named Carol, Mallory and Niaj before they spoke. Dave's timeline correction flipped the Grace trial and the later Heidi trial. On D4, Bob, Mallory and Frank had flipped and Niaj was confirmed Medic by Mallory's Pharmacist flip, so only Carol was left as the SK.

tip: Never fake a role that a living Village player is likely to hold and counterclaim, and never fake a token role beyond its token limit. If you visited a watched target, a cover like 'Vanilla, no action' isn't available. Pick a claim that has no living counterpart, or one whose results can't be checked.
evidence: Mallory's Medic claim ran into Niaj's real Medic claim. Bob's Sheriff claim ran into Frank, who checked him and got Evil. Judy claimed Surveyor and reported three results from a two-token role. Her late switch to Roleplayer convinced nobody, and she was hanged D5.

tip: Don't vote as a block. Once one teammate flips, every shared Guilty or Innocent vote becomes the town's case against the rest. When a teammate's trial is clearly lost, it can be better to vote Guilty with the town.
evidence: Bob, Judy and Mallory all voted Guilty on the real Lookout Grace and No/Innocent on Bob. After Bob and Mallory flipped, Dave and Erin cited exactly these votes to hang Judy.

tip: Once the Medic is identified, have your role-blocker block them every night you attack a protected-looking target. Also expect a neutral killer to be hunting the same loud information roles. Spread your attack to a second high-value target so both kills don't land on the same player.
evidence: Mallory blocked Niaj on N2 and N3, which stopped his Strong protections on Grace and Frank. But Carol's SK attack hit the same target both nights, so the Katana added no extra kills and the Village kept its numbers.

tip: Shoot the player a confirmed or near-confirmed report places on a victim, especially when that player is one of two people claiming the same role. A Basic shot (1 token) kills most roles, which have no Defense. Save the rest unless you suspect a Neutral with innate Defense.
evidence: Erin shot Mallory, who was on Grace's list and the duplicate Medic claimant. She was the Pharmacist and the Katana holder. It worked, but Erin spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot when Basic would have done.

tip: When two players claim Sheriff and share a result on a player who flipped Good, the shared result confirms neither of them. Break the tie with an independent check of one claimant, and look at who visited the framed player.
evidence: Bob and Frank both said Alice was Evil. Alice had been framed by Bob, which is also why she read Evil. Frank's N2 check on Bob (Evil) plus Bob's Guilty vote on Grace got Bob hanged, and he flipped Fabricator.
